1:
Dating the subjugation divides the sources. Ellicott puts it in Jehoiakim's fifth or sixth year, since Nebuchadnezzar had beaten Necho at Carchemish in the fourth and was called home by his father Nabopolassar's death; Jehoiakim submitted, was put in chains, lost some Temple treasures, was left on his throne as a vassal, paid tribute three years and then tried to throw off the yoke. Delitzsch takes Daniel's third year as no more than the extreme terminus from which to count, puts Carchemish early in the fourth year and the taking of Jerusalem in the same year. Gill agrees on the date and adds the hostages — Daniel and his companions, carried off with some vessels of the temple — and the restoration on promise of obedience. Clarke adds that Nebuchadnezzar, sent by his father against revolted provinces, took Carchemish and all that Egypt held from the Euphrates to the Nile, and reduced Necho's tributary to himself.

Henry reads the revolt as folly: had Jehoiakim served his God he would not have served Babylon, and had he kept his word his condition would have been no worse. The bands were Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites, in Babylon's pay and showing their old enmity to the Israel of God; no commission from Nebuchadnezzar is mentioned, only one from the King of kings, since many serve God's purposes unaware. Two intentions he finds: the punishment of Manasseh's sins after long waiting for a repentance that never came, the innocent blood singled out as unpardoned, remitted as to temporal penalty only, national sins lying charged on the land; and the fulfilling of the prophecies. Ellicott traces the revolt to Egyptian instigation and the raiders to hereditary enemies reprising Josiah's power over them, names the prophets behind the word of the Lord — Isaiah, Micah, Urijah, Huldah, Jeremiah, Habakkuk and others unrecorded — and renders the clause strictly: only upon the mouth of Jehovah did it happen, though LXX and Syriac read wrath for mouth, which Ewald prefers. Out of his sight he glosses from the Targum as the land where God dwelt in his Temple, and he refuses Bähr's softening of the charge into mere persistence in Manasseh's kind of sin: the blood cried to heaven, and children suffering for fathers was precisely the Old Testament doctrine until Ezekiel proclaimed another. Delitzsch adds that Jehovah would not forgive though Moses and Samuel had interceded. Clarke points back to Huldah; Wesley makes the sins properly Judah's own, Manasseh's only as they repeated them.

Of the remaining acts Ellicott gathers, with Hitzig, that Habakkuk's woe on building high describes exactions of forced labour on the city defences, and reports Thenius's guess that the fortress on Ophel was enlarged. The omitted burial notice they all read as significant. Ellicott sets Jeremiah's sentence beside it — not lamented, buried with the burial of an ass, cast beyond the gates — and takes Jehoiakim to have fallen among the freebooters, his body left where it lay, and holds, against Thenius, that the words imply no peaceful death. Delitzsch says the contradiction with Jeremiah is now generally given up, since Michaelis and Winer, but finds their solution insufficient. Gill has him die at the gates as soon as he came out, unburied, with temple vessels lodged in the idol's house at Babylon and Eupolemus reporting the gold, silver and brass carried off, and passes on Lyra's reading of the marks found in his body as idolatrous. Clarke will scarcely reckon Jehoiachin's three months a reign, so that Jeremiah's word stands and the throne was Babylon's. On Egypt, Henry sees the late oppressor of Israel disabled from recovering his losses or helping his allies; Ellicott measures the loss to the torrent of Egypt, the Wady-el-Arish, and observes that before Carchemish Necho had held all Syria and the land east of Jordan, so that Judah faced its revolt with no help left.
8:
The king's age at accession is the first crux. Gill holds that eighteen and eight can both stand: Jehoiachin was made king alongside his father in that father's first year, so that he was eight when he began to reign with him and eighteen when he began to reign alone. He reports a second solution, that the eight marks the eighth year of the captivity of Judah, and then concludes that the copyist very probably wrote eight for eighteen, since the Arabic and Syriac read eighteen there as here. Wesley takes the co-regency without qualification, noting that other kings of Israel and Judah had done the same in times of trouble. Clarke will not reconcile the figures at all but calls the shorter one corrupt, since a king carried to Babylon after three months had wives there, which a boy of eight or nine would not, and since of such an age it could scarcely be said that he did evil as a king. Ellicott counts four or five forms of the name, from the contraction in Ezekiel to the transposed and shortened forms in Jeremiah and finally Coniah, which Ewald thinks original while Hengstenberg has the prophet clipping it deliberately, leaving a confirming God without the will to confirm, to foreshadow the king's fate.

On the verdict Gill is brief: a partner in his father's throne was a partner in his sins. Ellicott weighs whether the lion of Ezekiel's parable is this king — Ewald among others refers it to him, but Thenius asks how, in ninety days of which a good part went in the siege, he could have done what is there described, and refers it with Hitzig to Zedekiah — and records that Josephus called him naturally good and just, probably on a misreading of Jeremiah. The siege itself the sources date and stage. Delitzsch glosses at that time as the moment Jehoiachin came to the throne, or, with the Chronicles, the turn of the year; Ellicott makes it the spring, passes on Thenius's inference that a cordon was drawn across the south country to cut off any succour from Egypt, takes the servants of the king to be his generals, and observes from the tense that the siege had begun before Nebuchadnezzar arrived. Gill says it more plainly: he came in person, following his army.

The surrender is read uniformly as despair and variously as policy. Clarke has him see that further defence was useless and give himself up hoping for better terms; Ellicott has him despair of the defence and throw himself on Nebuchadnezzar's clemency, with the queen-mother, his grandees and his courtiers beside him, probably hoping to keep his throne as a vassal of Babylon. Delitzsch agrees on the motive and supplies the answer: Nebuchadnezzar showed none of the favour he had shown Jehoiakim at the first taking of the city, but treated this king as a rebel, made him prisoner and carried him off with his mother, his wives, his princes and his chamberlains, as Jeremiah had prophesied; and the mother is named, he insists, for no such reason as the guardianship of a minor. Henry turns the moment into a reproach. Jehoiachin beat a parley and went out because the name of Babylon had grown formidable; had he made his peace with God and taken the method Hezekiah took in the like case he might have held out with courage, honour and success, one chasing a thousand, but wanting the faith and piety of an Israelite he had not the resolution of a man, of a soldier, or of a prince, and he and his house went out prisoners of war, as servants of sin do. Wesley adds that the surrender followed Jeremiah's counsel and was to the king's own good, and that the eighth year belongs to Nebuchadnezzar, since Jehoiachin did not reign half a year.
13:
Clarke sorts the plundering into three spoliations: the first under Jehoiakim, when the vessels taken were set in the temple of Nebuchadnezzar's god; the second here, when what remained was broken or cut in pieces; the third under Zedekiah, when the brass and the pillars went. Gill has the gates thrown open and the conqueror entering to strip palace and temple alike. Ellicott notes the entry is implied rather than stated, and finds it surprising that anything was left in the treasury after repeated spoliations — which argues for secret store-chambers and supports the chronicler's account of the sanctuary's wealth. The cutting in pieces he takes to mean the gold plating stripped from such vessels as the altar of incense, the table of shewbread and the Ark. Delitzsch reads the verb the same way, as bearing off the gold plates, and notes that the solid-gold vessels taken first — basins, scoops, goblets, knives, tongs — were later given back by Cyrus. Wesley asks how these survived earlier rifling by the kings of Egypt and Israel, and offers the priests' care, the clemency of conquerors, or a providence disposing their hearts to leave them.

The sweeping phrase, all agree, is limited by what follows. Gill makes it the chief, the honourable, the rich and the useful; Wesley the best and most considerable part; Delitzsch the whole population reduced, by the clause about the common people, to the cream of the citizens, with the king, the queen-mother and the wives held back for the later list. Ellicott defines the classes: the princes are the grandees of the court, some of the priests and the heads of the clans; the mighty men of valour he keeps as fighting men against Thenius and Bähr, who would have men of property; the craftsmen are workers in wood, stone and metal, the smiths properly those who shut, makers of bolts and bars, whose removal made further outbreaks impossible. He calls Kimchi's gloss, learned men who shut other mouths with riddles, a curiosity of exegesis, and judges the derivation Hitzig and Thenius propose a very surprising compound for Hebrew. The arithmetic he works out: seven thousand warriors and a thousand craftsmen leave two thousand aristocrats to fill out the ten, while Jeremiah's three thousand and twenty-three Thenius explains by a scribe confusing one numeral letter for another. Clarke and Wesley give the same two figures, Wesley adding that smiths could have furnished new arms and fresh trouble.

The particulars follow. Ellicott hears a different verb form and would render it yea, he carried away, the general statement now itemised; the carrying off of the king and the king's mother he reads as the fulfilment of Jeremiah, and the mighty of the land, the Targum's magnates, as those who had taken refuge in the city as the Chaldeans came up. Gill notes only that Jehoiachin remained in Babylon at least thirty-seven years. For the successor the sources differ on his place among Josiah's sons: Gill and Ellicott make Mattaniah the third, Delitzsch the youngest, ten at his father's death and twenty-one at his accession, who as uncle to a youth too young to have a son fit to reign had the first claim, and was set over the poor left behind. Clarke notes only that he was Josiah's son and Jehoiakim's brother. Ellicott adds that Jehoiachin was childless then though he had offspring in exile, that the Greek reading his son is a corruption of uncle, and that the new name turned a gift of Jah into Jah is righteousness — a change that Jeremiah's promise of a king called Jehovah our righteousness shows to have raised delusive expectations. Wesley makes the name an admonition of the justice that had punished Jehoiakim and would as surely overtake the same perfidiousness, and Ellicott suspects the clemency of setting up a native prince executed a promise made at the surrender.
18:
Gill opens the last reign with arithmetic, working back through the three months of Jehoahaz, the eleven years of Jehoiakim and the three months and ten days of his son to make Zedekiah between nine and ten years old when Josiah died. Delitzsch opens it with a question of sources, setting beside this section the historical appendix to the book of Jeremiah, which agrees with it for the most part word for word while omitting the murder of Gedaliah and the flight of the people to Egypt, and adding instead a computation of the numbers led away to Babylon. The variations he mostly puts down to copyists, but not all of them: the appendix carries notices about the vessels of the temple, and particularly about the ornaments of the brazen pillars, which appear nowhere in these books. That, he argues, settles the direction of dependence in both directions at once; neither was the text before us drawn from the appendix, nor the appendix borrowed from the books of Kings and added to the prophet's collection.

On the king's character the sources converge and then diverge on its bearing. Clarke finds it astonishing that not one of these kings took warning from the judgments which fell on his sinful predecessors. Ellicott asks that the prophet's own evidence be compared with the historian's verdict, points to Ezekiel for a vivid reflection of the state of religion at the time and for the denunciation of Zedekiah's breach of faith with Babylon, and observes that the comparison here is drawn with Jehoiakim, not with Jehoiachin, who reigned only three months. Delitzsch presses the theological point that the verdict is not meant to make God the author of the man's wickedness: the thing which came to pass by divine anger was that such a king came to the throne at all, a man, on the judgment of Brentius which he passes on, simple and dependent upon his counsellors and at the same time despising the word of God and impenitent, and so the cause of Jerusalem's destruction. Ellicott says the same from the other side, that the raising of such a prince was itself a token of displeasure, since his character could only hasten the end.

The rebellion is where Ellicott does most work. He renders the clause literally, that upon the anger of Jehovah it befell Jerusalem, and would put a full stop before the last sentence, so that the rebellion is stated on its own and not as the thing which the anger brought about. Behind it he sets the whole diplomacy: Zedekiah looked for help from Pharaoh Hophra, called Apries, and sent ambassadors to him; Edom, Ammon and Moab, with Tyre and Zidon, were eager to be rid of the Babylonian yoke and had proposed a general rising; the hopes those negotiations raised can be measured by the prophecy of Hananiah; and Jeremiah opposed the whole project to the utmost of his power, the event proving him right. He adds that early in the reign Zedekiah had tried to procure the return of those carried away under his predecessor, and that in his fourth year he went to Babylon himself, perhaps on the same errand and to satisfy Nebuchadnezzar of his loyalty, so that the date of the open revolt cannot now be fixed. Clarke dates it to the eighth year, reproves the breaking of the oath sworn to Babylon, and calls it the filling up of the measure of iniquity; Delitzsch notes only that the oath had been sworn by God. Wesley draws the moral backwards: the people's sins were the true cause why God gave them wicked kings and suffered them to do wickedly, that they might bring the long-deserved and threatened punishment upon themselves and upon their people.
